segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I am speaking the truth in Christ, I am not lying, and my conscience bears witness with me in the Holy Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I could wish that I myself were accursed, cut off from Christ, for the sake of my brothers and sisters, my kin according to the flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They are Israelites; theirs are the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, comes the Christ, who is over all, God blessed forever. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israel,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: nor are they all children because they are Abraham’s offspring; rather,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “It is through Isaac that your offspring will be called.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God; rather, the children of the promise are counted as offspring.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this word was one of promise:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “About this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And not only that, but there is also Rebecca, who conceived by one man, our father Isaac.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when they were not yet born and had done nothing good or bad, so that God’s purpose in choosing might stand,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not by works but by the one who calls, it was said to her,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “The older will serve the younger.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he says to Moses,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will have mercy on whomever I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whomever I have compassion.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, it depends not on the one who wants or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the Scripture says to Pharaoh,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might display my power in you, and so that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, he has mercy on whom he wants, and he hardens whom he wants.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You will say to me then,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why then does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But who are you, O human being, to answer back to God? Will what is formed say to the one who formed it,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Why did you make me like this?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or does the potter not have the right over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But what if God, wanting to display his wrath and make known his power, bore with great patience vessels of wrath made ready for destruction,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and did so to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand for glory—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: us, whom he also called, not only from among Jews but also from among Gentiles?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he also says in Hosea:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I will call those who are not my people ‘my people,’ and her who is not beloved ‘beloved’;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: and it will be that in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be like the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved;

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: for the Lord will carry out his word on the earth, completing it and cutting it short.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And as Isaiah said beforehand:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “If the Lord of Hosts had not left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say? That Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness, the righteousness that is by faith;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not reach that law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Why? Because they pursued it not by faith but as if by works. They stumbled over the stumbling stone,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Look, I am laying in Zion a stumbling stone and a rock that makes people fall, and the one who believes in him will not be put to shame.”

notes.note: In the Septuagint this word names something handed over to God for destruction and so removed from ordinary use. Paul says he would accept that fate, separated from Christ, if it could benefit his fellow Israelites; many readers hear an echo of Moses' offer in Exodus 32:32. The verb rendered 'I could wish' can also mean 'pray', and its tense marks the wish as one that cannot actually be carried out.

notes.phrase: who is over all, God blessed forever
notes.traditional: who is over all, God blessed for ever
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts had no punctuation, and the sentence can be divided in two ways. As rendered here, following the punctuation of the SBLGNT, the words describe Christ and call him God. The alternative puts a full stop after 'the Christ' (or after 'over all') and reads the rest as a separate blessing: 'God who is over all be blessed forever.' The grammar is often judged to favour the first reading, but the question remains disputed, partly because Paul seldom if ever calls Christ 'God' so directly elsewhere.

The Greek word is literally 'seed', a singular noun used collectively for descendants. 'Offspring' keeps the collective singular without the archaic sound of 'seed'; it is used for the same word in verses 8 and 29. The verb 'called' in this quotation from Genesis 21:12 is the same one Paul uses for God's calling in verses 12 and 24 to 26.

notes.traditional: the purpose of God according to election
notes.note: The Greek noun means a choice or selection. The traditional 'election' is accurate as a technical term, but in modern English it suggests voting. Most scholars agree that the phrase describes a purpose of God that operates by his own choice, which is what the rendering here expresses.

The quotation is Malachi 1:2-3, where Jacob and Esau stand for the nations Israel and Edom. In biblical idiom 'love' and 'hate' set side by side often express preference for one over another, not emotional hostility (compare Genesis 29:30-31 and Luke 14:26). How far that softens the statement here is debated; the plain word is kept in the text.

The Greek participle leaves the logical connection open. It may mean 'because he wanted' to display his wrath, so that the patience served that display. Or it may mean 'although he wanted' to, so that the patience held it back. The rendering keeps the Greek's openness. The sentence in verses 22 to 24 is also unfinished in Greek, an 'if' with no conclusion, which is why it is rendered 'what if'.

The Greek form can be passive ('made ready', without saying by whom) or middle ('having made themselves ready'). Paul uses a different and explicitly active verb for the vessels of mercy, 'which he prepared beforehand'. Some interpreters take the contrast as deliberate; others hold that God is the implied agent in both cases. The rendering leaves the agent unstated, as the Greek does.

The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it refers to the non-Jewish peoples, for which English uses 'Gentiles'. It is the same word that is translated 'nations' elsewhere in the New Testament.

notes.phrase: completing it and cutting it short
notes.traditional: For he will finish the work, and cut it short in righteousness: because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth
notes.note: Many later manuscripts have a longer form of this verse, closer to the Greek of Isaiah 10:22-23, and the King James Version follows it. The earliest witnesses have the shorter text translated here. The Greek is compressed and its sense is uncertain: 'word' may mean God's sentence or reckoning, and the two participles may describe carrying it out completely and swiftly.

Paul's Greek, following the Septuagint of Isaiah 1:9, leaves the Hebrew word tseva'ot untranslated as 'Sabaoth'. It means 'armies' or 'hosts', and the title presents God as commander of the heavenly armies. It is translated here because 'Sabaoth' is easily mistaken for 'Sabbath'.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The 'injustice' denied of God in verse 14 is the negative of the same word. 'Righteousness' is kept here for being in the right before God; some scholars prefer 'justice' or 'covenant faithfulness'.

notes.phrase: a rock that makes people fall
notes.note: The Greek word refers to something that trips a person up or traps them. 'Offence' now suggests hurt feelings, which is not the meaning. The quotation combines Isaiah 28:16 with a phrase from Isaiah 8:14, so that the foundation stone God lays in Zion is also the stone people stumble over.

The Greek pronoun can mean 'him' or 'it', that is, the stone. Paul quotes the line again at 10:11 with clear reference to Christ, so most interpreters take the stone here as Christ, and the rendering follows them. The verb is from the same word-family as 'faith' in verses 30 and 32 and could also be translated 'trusts'.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout Paul with senses ranging from physical descent to the sphere opposed to the Spirit; translators vary between 'flesh', 'human descent' and 'sinful nature', and readers need to see when it is one word.
The plural is used across the New Testament for mixed groups of believers or kin, and the choice between 'brothers' and 'brothers and sisters' should be made once.
The collective singular 'seed' carries arguments in Romans 4, Romans 9 and Galatians 3, so 'seed', 'offspring' and 'descendants' should not alternate between chapters.
With ἐκλεκτός and ἐκλέγομαι it forms the 'election/chosen' family, where 'election' now misleads; one rendering is needed across Romans 9 and 11, 1 Thessalonians and 2 Peter.

candidates.rendering: a rock that makes people fall (stumbling/falling language)
candidates.reason: The traditional 'offence' and 'stumbling block' both recur across the Gospels and Paul, along with the verb σκανδαλίζω; a consistent trip-and-fall rendering needs to be set once.
